language.name: German
language.variety: Standard German · formal Sie · minimal production grammar
features: Statements: subject + finite verb + rest; yes/no questions begin with the finite verb.
Completed past events: haben/sein + participle. Simple states often use war/hatte.
Future plans: present tense + morgen/nächste Woche/bald; no future conjugation required.
With können/wollen/müssen, the second verb stays in the infinitive at the end.
For simple reasons use denn, which preserves ordinary main-clause word order.

lessons.title: Begin a conversation
lessons.goal: Greet someone, be polite, and end an exchange
lessons.introduction: Keep a handful of social formulas as complete units. The rest of the manual builds productive sentences.

notes.recipe: Polite formula → short statement → question.
notes.explanation: Learn greetings and thanks as conventional units. Make new statements with subject + conjugated verb + rest.
notes.detail: Sie is the formal you, suitable for a shop, workplace or unfamiliar person. Sie usually takes the same verb form as wir: Sie haben, wir haben.
notes.caution: The guide focuses on production, not understanding every reply. Ask for slower speech when needed.

lessons.title: People and simple states
lessons.goal: Say who is doing something and describe a current state
lessons.introduction: Change the subject or quality while keeping the same sentence skeleton.

notes.recipe: ich / Sie / wir / er + verb + complement
notes.explanation: The subject identifies who performs an action. In a normal statement the conjugated verb comes second.
notes.detail: A small set of high-frequency forms goes a long way: ich bin, Sie sind, wir sind, er ist; ich wohne, Sie wohnen. Learn adjectives such as müde and bereit without adjective endings after sein.
notes.caution: The ordinary word order is subject + finite verb + rest. When a time word comes first, the finite verb still comes second.

lessons.title: Needs and possessions
lessons.goal: Communicate everyday needs and what you have
lessons.introduction: Change the object, not the entire sentence. Learn the short noun phrase together with its article.

notes.recipe: Ich brauche / habe / möchte + noun phrase
notes.explanation: A reusable verb takes many interchangeable objects. Memorize noun gender as part of each noun, not a separate article chart.
notes.detail: German changes the article of many masculine objects: ein Termin → einen Termin, ein Kaffee → einen Kaffee. Neuter ein Ticket and feminine eine Frage are unchanged in the accusative. Two objects use zwei + plural.
notes.caution: Do not add ein to mass nouns such as Wasser, Geld or Zeit in these constructions.

lessons.title: Ask simple questions
lessons.goal: Ask for confirmation, locations, and prices
lessons.introduction: A question changes sentence structure. It should not require learning a separate phrase for every verb.

notes.recipe: Finite verb + subject + rest + ?
notes.explanation: Make a yes/no question by moving the finite verb to the front. This rule also works with the past auxiliary and modal verbs.
notes.detail: Wo ist …? asks for a location; Wie viel kostet …? asks for a price. These two question families are useful enough to learn separately.
notes.caution: There is no equivalent of English do in ordinary German yes/no questions.

examples.english: How much does a coffee cost?
How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a book cost?

lessons.title: Say what is not true
lessons.goal: Refuse, correct information, and say what you lack
lessons.introduction: Negation is a reusable operator over a clause; noun and verb negation differ between languages.

notes.recipe: nicht (action/state) / kein + noun
notes.explanation: Use nicht for a verb or state. Use forms of kein when saying that you do not have, need or buy an indefinite thing.
notes.detail: Examples of the noun pattern: kein Ticket, keine Zeit, keinen Termin. These follow the same gender and case distinctions as ein. Nicht often stands before the last infinitive or after an adjective.
notes.caution: Nicht and kein are not interchangeable. Learn the highest-frequency noun chunks first.

examples.english: I do not have a ticket.
I do not have an appointment.
I do not understand a question.

lessons.title: Get around
lessons.goal: Find destinations and describe movement
lessons.introduction: Destinations are semantic slots. A language determines the preposition and article for each place.

notes.recipe: Wo ist …? / Ich gehe + direction / Ich bleibe + location.
notes.explanation: Movement and position are different roles; learn the destination phrase as a reusable unit.
notes.detail: Use nach Hause when going home, but zu Hause when staying at home. Typical destinations include zum Bahnhof, zur Apotheke, ins Büro and ins Krankenhaus.
notes.caution: German prepositions choose cases. Our profile packages common places with their prepositions to postpone that bigger system.

lessons.title: Describe ordinary life
lessons.goal: Talk about working, eating, drinking, and learning
lessons.introduction: Reuse the present tense for common activities and the things that go with them.

notes.recipe: Subject + present-tense verb + object.
notes.explanation: The present tense covers everyday routines: work, learn, eat, drink, take transport and speak a language.
notes.detail: An infinitive usually ends in -en. With ich, the present often ends in -e; with Sie/wir, it resembles the infinitive. Frequent verbs such as essen, nehmen and sprechen are irregular for er.
notes.caution: Do not expect every verb to conjugate regularly. Memorize the few common irregular verbs the guide actually uses.

lessons.title: Can, cannot, and requests
lessons.goal: Ask permission, offer help, and describe ability
lessons.introduction: Modal verbs attach to an action. The action stays an infinitive in many languages.

notes.recipe: Ich kann + ... + infinitive. / Können Sie ... ?
notes.explanation: The modal können is conjugated; the main verb stays at the end in the infinitive. Add bitte to make a request courteous.
notes.detail: A reliable request is Können Sie mir bitte helfen? Here mir is dative because helfen selects a dative recipient. The same skeleton works with kommen, warten, bezahlen and anrufen.
notes.caution: Do not conjugate both verbs. After können, use helfen rather than helfe.

lessons.title: Want and have to
lessons.goal: Communicate obligations, desires, and basic plans
lessons.introduction: Ability, desire, and obligation differ in meaning but share a reusable modal construction.

notes.recipe: Ich will / muss + ... + infinitive.
notes.explanation: Wollen expresses intention; müssen expresses obligation. They share the same final-infinitive structure as können.
notes.detail: Short independent statements are enough: Ich muss heute arbeiten. Ich will morgen zum Bahnhof gehen. When asking a stranger for an item, ich möchte is softer than ich will.
notes.caution: Negated müssen does not necessarily mean must not. Ich muss nicht often means do not have to.

examples.english: I have to go to the hospital.
I have to go to the office.
I have to go to the station.
I want to buy a ticket.
I want to buy a book.

lessons.title: Today and now
lessons.goal: Attach simple time information without changing the central event
lessons.introduction: Time is an operator on a whole statement. Keep the main sentence shape familiar.

notes.recipe: Subject + finite verb + heute/jetzt + rest.
notes.explanation: Time is added to a sentence without changing its basic grammatical structure.
notes.detail: Heute is today and jetzt is now. In a simple main clause the finite verb stays second regardless of whether the time expression appears early or late.
notes.caution: German morgen (tomorrow) is lowercase. Morgen (morning) is a noun.

lessons.title: Yesterday: things you did
lessons.goal: Describe completed actions and experiences
lessons.introduction: A useful language needs a real past. Learn one dependable past construction before chasing every literary form.

notes.recipe: Ich habe + ... + Partizip II. / Ich hatte ... / Ich war ...
notes.explanation: For completed spoken events, Perfekt is the high-utility past: a present form of haben/sein plus the past participle at the end.
notes.detail: Regular verbs often have ge-...-t: gekauft, gearbeitet. Others must be memorized: getrunken, gegessen, genommen. For past states, war and hatte are short and natural.
notes.caution: Not every participle uses ge-. Many verbs with inseparable prefixes use forms such as verstanden or bezahlt.

examples.target: Ich habe gestern ein Ticket gekauft.
Ich habe gestern einen Kaffee gekauft.
Ich habe gestern ein Buch gekauft.

lessons.title: Past journeys and contact
lessons.goal: Say where you went, who you called, and when you arrived
lessons.introduction: Movement verbs may choose a different auxiliary in the past. The shared meaning stays the same.

notes.recipe: Ich bin + ... + gegangen/gekommen/angekommen.
notes.explanation: Many movement and change-of-location verbs use sein rather than haben in the Perfekt.
notes.detail: Ich bin gestern zum Bahnhof gegangen. The finite auxiliary comes second; the participle ends the clause. Past telephone calls use haben: Ich habe Sie angerufen.
notes.caution: Do not translate English have mechanically. In this system, movement selects sein but ordinary actions select haben.

examples.target: Ich bin gestern nach Hause gegangen.

examples.english: I went to the station yesterday.
examples.target: Ich bin gestern zum Bahnhof gegangen.

examples.english: I went to the hospital yesterday.
examples.target: Ich bin gestern ins Krankenhaus gegangen.

examples.english: I stayed at the hotel last week.
examples.target: Ich bin letzte Woche im Hotel geblieben.

lessons.title: Tomorrow and next week
lessons.goal: Describe upcoming events and near-future plans
lessons.introduction: The goal is to express future meaning, not to memorize a full future-tense paradigm.

notes.recipe: Present tense + morgen / nächste Woche / bald.
notes.explanation: Everyday German frequently expresses a planned future with the present tense and an unambiguous time expression.
notes.detail: Ich gehe morgen ins Büro and Wir arbeiten nächste Woche are complete, normal future-oriented sentences. You can postpone the werden + infinitive future form.
notes.caution: Without a time marker, present tense may not communicate future meaning. The compiler supplies bald when none is given.

examples.english: I will go to the office tomorrow.
I will go to the station tomorrow.
I will go to the hotel tomorrow.
I will send a message tomorrow.

lessons.title: Compare past, now, and future
lessons.goal: Reuse the same action across three moments in time
lessons.introduction: These are inflection paradigms generated from one event. Notice what changes and what stays fixed.

notes.recipe: Today: present → Yesterday: Perfekt → Tomorrow: present + time.
notes.explanation: Keep the event and its object fixed and change only the temporal operator. This is the core of a usable narrative system.
notes.detail: Notice which verbs select habe and which select bin. Compare these patterns as grammar, not three unrelated phrases.
notes.caution: Full German past narrative style involves additional forms, but you do not need them for basic past conversations.

examples.target: Ich habe gestern ein Ticket gekauft.

examples.english: I will buy a ticket tomorrow.

examples.target: Ich habe gestern ein Buch gekauft.

examples.english: I will buy a book tomorrow.
I go to the station today.
I went to the station yesterday.
examples.target: Ich bin gestern zum Bahnhof gegangen.

examples.english: I will go to the station tomorrow.

examples.target: Ich bin gestern nach Hause gegangen.

lessons.title: Talk to and about people
lessons.goal: Mention another person, calls, and requests for help
lessons.introduction: The meaning includes both the actor and recipient. The language puts each in the right grammatical form.

notes.recipe: Subject + verb + recipient (mir / Ihnen / uns / ihm).
notes.explanation: The person performing an action and the person receiving it are separate semantic slots.
notes.detail: Helfen requires the dative: mir, Ihnen, uns, ihm. Anrufen takes an accusative object: mich, Sie, uns, ihn; it is separable in the present (ich rufe Sie an), but zusammen in the infinitive (anrufen).
notes.caution: Learn the case required by the verb, not just a translated pronoun.

lessons.title: Make everyday transactions
lessons.goal: Buy, pay, ask prices, and handle numbers
lessons.introduction: Transactions are composed from needs, quantities, questions, and payment methods.

notes.recipe: Ich möchte … / Ich brauche zwei … / Wie viel kostet …?
notes.explanation: Reuse nouns, quantities and the same two question patterns across different goods and services.
notes.detail: Zwei + plural avoids indefinite article endings. With card is mit Karte, cash is bar. Prices use a nominative subject: ein Ticket kostet, not einen Ticket kostet.
notes.caution: One coffee is einen Kaffee as an object, but ein Kaffee as the subject of kostet.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a coffee cost?
How much does a book cost?
How much does a room cost?
I did not buy a ticket yesterday.
examples.target: Ich habe gestern kein Ticket gekauft.

lessons.title: Describe problems and limits
lessons.goal: Explain illness, lack of time, and things that went wrong
lessons.introduction: Build a fact, then add a cause if needed. Use short separate clauses rather than intricate syntax.

notes.recipe: Ich bin krank. Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
notes.explanation: Two short correct statements communicate a problem. Avoid subordinate clauses until you actually need them.
notes.detail: A state uses sein + adjective; an inability uses können + nicht + infinitive. You can attach a reason to connect them without changing the construction.
notes.caution: A short message can be perfectly appropriate even without complex grammar or stylistic variety.

examples.english: I do not have a problem.
I do not have an appointment.
I cannot come today, because I am sick.
examples.target: Ich kann heute nicht kommen, denn ich bin krank.

examples.english: I cannot work, because I do not have time.
examples.target: Ich kann nicht arbeiten, denn ich habe keine Zeit.

examples.english: I need a ticket, but I do not have money.
examples.target: Ich brauche ein Ticket, aber ich habe kein Geld.

lessons.title: Give a reason without hard grammar
lessons.goal: Explain why you cannot do something or need a change
lessons.introduction: Use two simple main clauses linked by “because.” German can use denn rather than a weil subordinate clause.

notes.recipe: Independent clause + denn + independent clause.
notes.explanation: For a straightforward reason, denn is the simple option: both clauses retain ordinary main-clause word order.
notes.detail: Ich kann nicht kommen, denn ich bin krank. Unlike weil, denn does not send the conjugated verb to the end of the reason clause.
notes.caution: Denn is slightly more formal than conversational weil, but it stays understandable and grammatically simple.

examples.english: I cannot come, because I am sick.
examples.target: Ich kann nicht kommen, denn ich bin krank.

examples.english: I cannot help you, because I am busy.
examples.target: Ich kann Ihnen nicht helfen, denn ich bin beschäftigt.

examples.english: I cannot work, because I do not have time.
examples.target: Ich kann nicht arbeiten, denn ich habe keine Zeit.

examples.english: I need a ticket, but I do not have money.
examples.target: Ich brauche ein Ticket, aber ich habe kein Geld.

examples.english: I cannot go to the office today, because I am busy.
examples.target: Ich kann heute nicht ins Büro gehen, denn ich bin beschäftigt.

examples.english: I worked yesterday, and I will go to the office tomorrow.
examples.target: Ich habe gestern gearbeitet, und ich gehe morgen ins Büro.

lessons.title: Tell a small story
lessons.goal: Report a past event, a present situation, and a next step
lessons.introduction: A short narrative can be three independent simple sentences: yesterday, today, tomorrow.

notes.recipe: Gestern … . Heute … . Morgen … .
notes.explanation: Three short independent sentences can report a past event, explain today, and set up tomorrow.
notes.detail: Use Perfekt for yesterday’s action, present for today, and present with a future marker for tomorrow. The same verb-and-object blocks are reused.
notes.caution: This is a production strategy, not a claim that authentic German never uses longer sentences.

examples.english: I went to the hospital yesterday.
examples.target: Ich bin gestern ins Krankenhaus gegangen.

examples.english: I go to the hospital today.
I will go to the hospital tomorrow.
I will have an appointment tomorrow.

lessons.title: Your small communication system
lessons.goal: Combine the core blocks in work, errands, and personal communication
lessons.introduction: Choose a meaning, time, action and possible reason. The same operations produce many new statements.

notes.recipe: Who? + What? + When? + Not? + Can/Must? + Reason?
notes.explanation: Choose a small number of independent building blocks. The grammar adapts them into a correct, direct sentence.
notes.detail: For longer messages, prefer two or three short sentences to a complex subordinate construction. You can state a need, give a time and ask a question with no new grammar.
notes.caution: The manual teaches a deliberate expressive subset, not every natural alternative or full A2 reception and listening.

examples.english: I went to the office yesterday.
examples.target: Ich bin gestern ins Büro gegangen.

examples.english: I cannot come, because I am busy.
examples.target: Ich kann nicht kommen, denn ich bin beschäftigt.

examples.english: We will buy two tickets tomorrow.

lessons.title: Ask for missing information
lessons.goal: Ask what someone needs, has, or wants and how to get somewhere
lessons.introduction: Open questions are the same event with an unknown slot. Practise the question rule, not a list of shop phrases.

notes.recipe: Was + verb + subject? / Wie komme ich + destination?
notes.explanation: The missing information is one semantic slot. The question word replaces that slot, while the ordinary verb still changes for the speaker.
notes.detail: Was brauchen Sie? uses the conjugated verb directly after was. For a route: Wie komme ich zur Bank? The destination keeps its learned preposition.
notes.caution: Question constructions are not identical across languages. Reuse the target language’s question rule rather than translating English word order.

examples.english: How do I get to the station?
How do I get to the bank?
How do I get to the library?
How do I get to the hospital?

lessons.title: Talk about your habits
lessons.goal: Describe how often you study, travel, sleep and work
lessons.introduction: Attach a frequency operator to a present action. The same verb now communicates a routine rather than one event.

notes.recipe: Subject + finite verb + oft / jeden Tag + rest
notes.explanation: One frequency block can modify many present-tense events: often, sometimes, every day, every week. It describes habitual activity, not an individual finished action.
notes.detail: Frequency commonly appears after the finite verb: Ich lese oft ein Buch. With separable verbs, their particle still belongs at the end.
notes.caution: Avoid adding incompatible time operators, such as yesterday and every day, to the same single event.

examples.english: I take a bus every day.
examples.target: Ich nehme jeden Tag einen Bus.

examples.english: I take a train every day.
examples.target: Ich nehme jeden Tag einen Zug.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.goal: Express simple preferences and react to familiar things
lessons.introduction: Liking is one meaning with different grammar: compare what stays stable and what each language changes.

notes.recipe: Ich mag + noun / Ich mag ... nicht
notes.explanation: Expressing a preference is a reusable relation between a person and an object. You do not need a different complete sentence for every food or activity.
notes.detail: Mögen is irregular: ich mag, Sie mögen. For negating an indefinite thing, use kein in the appropriate form: Ich mag keinen Kaffee.
notes.caution: Spanish gustar reverses the typical English logic. The item liked controls the verb, while the person is a recipient.

lessons.title: Describe objects and places
lessons.goal: Say whether a thing is good, expensive, open or ready
lessons.introduction: Use a subject and a quality. German uses invariable adjectives here; French and Spanish handle agreement.

notes.recipe: Definite noun + ist / war + adjective
notes.explanation: A description joins an identifiable subject with a quality. This unlocks opinions about housing, prices, condition, and availability.
notes.detail: Predicative adjectives after sein have no ending: Das Zimmer ist groß. Negate the quality with nicht: Das Zimmer ist nicht teuer.
notes.caution: Learn which qualities belong to which things. An automatic adjective swap is not always a meaningful sentence.

lessons.title: Talk about housing
lessons.goal: Look for an apartment, describe a room, and ask about availability
lessons.introduction: A housing conversation uses the same operators: need, search, describe, and ask whether something exists.

notes.recipe: Ich suche + Wohnung / Die Wohnung ist + quality
notes.explanation: A practical housing conversation uses search, need, description, and availability. They are productive sentence families, not an apartment vocabulary script.
notes.detail: Suchen takes an accusative object: Ich suche eine Wohnung. In a description, use the nominative definite noun: Die Wohnung ist klein.
notes.caution: For detailed leases and legal commitments you will need vocabulary beyond this minimal guide.

examples.english: I will reserve a room next week.
examples.target: Ich reserviere nächste Woche ein Zimmer.

lessons.title: Find what is nearby
lessons.goal: Ask whether a bank, pharmacy, doctor or other service exists nearby
lessons.introduction: An existence statement is not a memorized location question. Change either the item or its location.

notes.recipe: Gibt es hier + noun? / Hier gibt es + noun
notes.explanation: Existence and location are different questions. First ask if a service exists; then ask where it is.
notes.detail: Es gibt takes an accusative noun: Gibt es hier eine Apotheke? Negative is es gibt keine Apotheke.
notes.caution: The most natural location prepositions and articles are language-specific. Learn them with their place names.

examples.english: Is there a café at the station?
examples.target: Gibt es am Bahnhof ein Café?

examples.english: Is there a shop at the station?
examples.target: Gibt es am Bahnhof ein Geschäft?

examples.english: Is there a restaurant at the station?
examples.target: Gibt es am Bahnhof ein Restaurant?

examples.english: There is a room at the hotel.
examples.target: Im Hotel gibt es ein Zimmer.

examples.english: There is a restaurant at the hotel.
examples.target: Im Hotel gibt es ein Restaurant.

examples.english: There is no bus stop here.

lessons.title: Ask the way and get there
lessons.goal: Ask how to reach places and say where you are going
lessons.introduction: Combine a route question with a movement frame. Each language supplies its own preposition.

notes.recipe: Wo ist + place? / Wie komme ich + destination?
notes.explanation: A location question asks where. A route question asks how to get there. Both can be combined with a statement of where you are going.
notes.detail: The destination preposition varies: zur Bank, zum Bahnhof, ins Stadtzentrum. The question Wie komme ich… remains unchanged.
notes.caution: These patterns ask for directions but do not yet teach you to understand every spoken route explanation.

examples.english: How do I get to the station?
How do I get to the pharmacy?
How do I get to the post office?
How do I get to the city centre?
How do I get to the café?
How do I get to the library?
How do I get to the bus stop?
I go to the city centre.
We will go to the station tomorrow.
We will go to the airport tomorrow.

lessons.title: Food, cafés and restaurants
lessons.goal: Buy basics, ask about prices and handle a restaurant visit
lessons.introduction: Reuse needs, prices, purchases, and reservations rather than learning a fixed restaurant dialogue.

notes.recipe: Ich möchte + item / Ich reserviere + item / Wie viel kostet ...?
notes.explanation: The same small grammar covers common food purchases, price checks, paying, and booking a table.
notes.detail: Möchten makes a request softer than wollen. Masculine objects often take einen, but prices use a nominative subject.
notes.caution: Words like bill and reservation are normal nouns here; they do not exempt a sentence from ordinary articles and word order.

examples.english: I will reserve a table tonight.
examples.target: Ich reserviere heute Abend einen Tisch.

examples.english: How much does a coffee cost?
How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a room cost?

lessons.title: Work and education
lessons.goal: Look for work, arrange meetings, and discuss everyday study
lessons.introduction: Introduce a useful job vocabulary through existing past, present, future, and question patterns.

notes.recipe: Ich suche / habe + noun; Ich arbeite jeden Tag
notes.explanation: Describe your job, daily routine, email tasks, and future meetings with the same core operators.
notes.detail: Ich suche einen Job, but ich habe eine Besprechung. Learn each noun with gender, then reuse present, Perfekt and future markers.
notes.caution: Simple workplace communication is not the same as understanding specialist professional or legal language.

examples.target: Ich habe gestern eine E-Mail geschrieben.

examples.english: I will meet a colleague tomorrow.

lessons.title: Messages and technology
lessons.goal: Explain what you can open, read, write, send and use
lessons.introduction: Digital communication uses the same verbs and objects as ordinary conversation.

notes.recipe: Ich benutze / lese / schreibe / sende + object
notes.explanation: Use, read, write and send are productive actions. Recombine them with electronic objects and time operators.
notes.detail: Benutzen and schreiben take direct objects. Ich habe eine E-Mail geschrieben uses the haben + participle past.
notes.caution: Avoid translating technical terms word for word across countries; each language uses its everyday terms here.

examples.english: I will write an email tomorrow.
I will write a message tomorrow.
I do not understand the information.

lessons.title: Forms and documents
lessons.goal: Ask for documents, complete a form, and explain what you signed
lessons.introduction: Administrative tasks can be communicated with small verb frames and the past operator.

notes.recipe: Ich fülle das Formular aus / Ich habe ... ausgefüllt
notes.explanation: Paperwork tasks need few new action frames: fill out, sign, read, and send. Attach time and requests as before.
notes.detail: Ausfüllen is separable: the particle goes to the end in ordinary present clauses. Its past participle is ausgefüllt.
notes.caution: A language guide cannot determine which documents a particular office legally requires.

examples.target: Ich habe gestern ein Dokument unterschrieben.
Ich habe gestern ein Formular unterschrieben.

examples.english: Can you read a document, please?
examples.target: Können Sie ein Dokument bitte lesen?

examples.english: I will send a document tomorrow.

lessons.title: Health and medicine
lessons.goal: Explain illness and find simple medical assistance
lessons.introduction: Use state + need + destination. Short truthful statements are often easier than complex medical descriptions.

notes.recipe: Ich bin krank / Ich brauche + noun / Ich gehe + place
notes.explanation: Describe a basic state, request help, and locate medical services using familiar structures.
notes.detail: Krank is an adjective after bin. Ich brauche einen Arzt uses accusative; zur Apotheke is a destination phrase.
notes.caution: The guide does not teach diagnosis, emergency instructions, or how to understand a clinician’s full response.

examples.english: I will meet a doctor tomorrow.
I cannot come, because I am sick.
examples.target: Ich kann nicht kommen, denn ich bin krank.

lessons.title: Appointments and services
lessons.goal: Make a plan, ask for help, cancel a meeting and reschedule simply
lessons.introduction: Use short independent sentences to explain a change of plans; do not start with formal subordinate clauses.

notes.recipe: Ich habe / sage ... ab / Ich kann nicht kommen, denn ...
notes.explanation: Appointments are nouns. Cancelling, reserving, and explaining a conflict are ordinary verb operators, not special scripts.
notes.detail: Absagen is separable in the present: Ich sage den Termin ab. Use Perfekt abgesagt for a completed cancellation.
notes.caution: In many circumstances an earlier or more polite written message is appropriate; short statements are a minimal oral baseline.

examples.target: Ich habe gestern einen Termin abgesagt.

examples.english: I will reserve a room next week.
examples.target: Ich reserviere nächste Woche ein Zimmer.

examples.english: I will reserve a table next week.
examples.target: Ich reserviere nächste Woche einen Tisch.

examples.english: I cannot come, because I am busy.
examples.target: Ich kann nicht kommen, denn ich bin beschäftigt.

lessons.title: People and social plans
lessons.goal: Say who you will see, whom you are waiting for, and what happened
lessons.introduction: A person can fill a semantic participant or an object slot. Each language handles pronouns and articles differently.

notes.recipe: Ich treffe + person / Ich warte auf + person
notes.explanation: Meeting, calling, and waiting are built from the same participants and objects as other actions.
notes.detail: Treffen takes accusative. Warten takes auf + accusative: Ich warte auf einen Freund. Past anrufen uses angerufen.
notes.caution: Social register varies by region. This guide consistently uses formal second-person forms for unfamiliar people.

examples.english: I will meet a friend tomorrow.
I will meet a colleague tomorrow.

examples.target: Wir haben ihm letzte Woche geholfen.

lessons.title: Lost things and problems
lessons.goal: Describe what you lost, what you are looking for, and whether you found it
lessons.introduction: Past + negative + object can communicate most basic lost-property problems.

notes.recipe: Ich habe + noun + verloren / Ich suche + noun
notes.explanation: Say what happened, what you are looking for, and what you could not find. Reuse the same semantic object in different verbs.
notes.detail: Verloren is the irregular past participle of verlieren. A second sentence can say what you are doing now: Ich suche einen Reisepass.
notes.caution: For an official loss report you may need more precise identity details beyond this minimal inventory.

examples.target: Ich habe gestern eine Geldbörse verloren.
Ich habe gestern einen Reisepass verloren.

lessons.title: Transport, waiting and delays
lessons.goal: Wait for transport, say when you left, and ask where to go
lessons.introduction: A travel problem is often a short sequence: movement, delay or waiting, next action.

notes.recipe: Ich warte auf den Bus / Ich bin gestern weggegangen
notes.explanation: Use movement, waiting, time, and location. A short description of a delay can be understood without complex syntax.
notes.detail: Warten auf takes accusative; many movement verbs form Perfekt with sein. A separable prefix rejoins the participle.
notes.caution: Timetables, platform changes and rapid announcements may still be hard to understand; ask for repetition.

examples.english: We will come back next week.
How do I get to the station?
How do I get to the bus stop?
How do I get to the airport?
We will go to the airport tomorrow.
We will go to the station tomorrow.

lessons.title: Tell more about the past
lessons.goal: Recount reading, writing, meeting people and losing belongings
lessons.introduction: The past operator does not depend on a particular topic. Change the action, keep the same temporal rule.

notes.recipe: haben/sein + participle; short states: war / hatte
notes.explanation: Once you know one past construction, many new events become possible without new sentence templates.
notes.detail: Ich habe gelesen, ich habe geschrieben and ich bin zurückgekommen share auxiliary + participle. Movement selects sein.
notes.caution: Real languages have more than one past tense. MVL teaches a dependable limited contrast, not every narrative nuance.

lessons.title: Make fuller plans
lessons.goal: Talk about documents, work and appointments next week or next month
lessons.introduction: Keep the event unchanged; attach the future operator and a time marker.

notes.recipe: Present verb + time in the future
notes.explanation: Reuse the future operator with different subjects, objects, and time markers to communicate personal plans.
notes.detail: Morgen, nächste Woche or nächsten Monat usually makes the present unambiguously future-facing. You can postpone werden.
notes.caution: Plans can change; future meaning in this manual generally assumes an intended event, not a promise or guarantee.

lessons.title: Connect several simple sentences
lessons.goal: Tell a short personal story with yesterday, today and tomorrow
lessons.introduction: Use two or three complete main clauses in order. You do not need a complex subordinate clause to be understood.

notes.recipe: Gestern habe/bin ... . Heute ... . Morgen ... .
notes.explanation: Two or three independent sentences are enough to give a sequence: what happened, what is happening, and what you will do.
notes.detail: Keep every sentence as a main clause; German finite-verb-second word order remains unchanged across sentences.
notes.caution: A fluent narrative has richer connections, but this deliberately restricted structure is a reliable starting point.

examples.english: I lost a passport yesterday. I look for a passport. I will go to the bank tomorrow.
examples.target: Ich habe gestern einen Reisepass verloren. Ich suche einen Reisepass. Ich gehe morgen zur Bank.

examples.english: I worked yesterday. I am tired. I will sleep tonight.
examples.target: Ich habe gestern gearbeitet. Ich bin müde. Ich schlafe heute Abend.

examples.english: I have a meeting today. I will write an email tomorrow.
examples.target: Ich habe heute eine Besprechung. Ich schreibe morgen eine E-Mail.

examples.english: I met a friend last week. We cooked. I will meet a friend next week.
examples.target: Ich habe letzte Woche einen Freund getroffen. Wir haben gekocht. Ich treffe nächste Woche einen Freund.

lessons.title: Apply your everyday grammar
lessons.goal: Put needs, time, problems and plans together independently
lessons.introduction: The final unit reuses the same core rules across several different situations. Review weak spots and change the semantic slots yourself.

notes.recipe: Person + action + object + optional time, NOT, CAN, reason
notes.explanation: Combine the small rules across new topics without rebuilding the sentence from a phrasebook entry.
notes.detail: After the core patterns are learned, swapping nouns and verbs is a question of semantic compatibility and a few irregular inflections.
notes.caution: A2-like productive coverage does not guarantee A2 proficiency. You must also practice understanding real speech and written texts.
